stem: A liver transplant recipient develops rising liver function tests after discharge. According to standard post-transplant monitoring references, what is the MOST appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.text: Liver biopsy when LFT elevation suggests a possible rejection episode
Permanent cessation of all immunosuppression without team evaluation
Ignore LFT changes because they never relate to graft status
Routine biopsy on day 7 for every recipient regardless of laboratory values

explanation.rationale_correct: Most centers biopsy when rising liver function tests suggest a possible rejection episode, although some centers may routinely biopsy on a set postoperative day.

rationale_incorrect.B: Rising LFTs prompt diagnostic evaluation and coordinated treatment decisions, not unilateral immunosuppression cessation.
rationale_incorrect.C: LFT trends are monitored because they may indicate rejection or other graft problems.
rationale_incorrect.D: Routine day-7 biopsy is practiced at some centers, but the question describes LFT-driven biopsy indication, not universal protocol regardless of labs.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 12, Liver Transplantation → Liver Biopsy → A.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: biopsy when there is a rise in LFTs suggesting a possible rejection episode

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 12 → Liver Biopsy → A. (biopsy when LFT rise suggests rejection); PDF p. 669 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Third 030100 item; liver LFT monitoring angle distinct from cctc-3001/3011; anchor verified on Cupples p. 669.

stem: A kidney recipient develops fever shortly after a suspected acute rejection episode is treated. Which mechanism BEST explains fever in this context?

options.text: Cytokine release during the rejection process
Complete absence of any immune activity in rejection
Fever that never occurs with acute rejection
Permanent fever that cannot respond to corticosteroid therapy

explanation.rationale_correct: Cytokine release during acute rejection is responsible for fever often associated with rejection episodes, and this fever typically resolves rapidly when high-dose corticosteroids are administered.

rationale_incorrect.B: Rejection involves immune activation and cytokine release, not absence of immune activity.
rationale_incorrect.C: Fever is commonly associated with acute rejection.
rationale_incorrect.D: Rejection-related fever often responds rapidly to high-dose corticosteroids rather than being permanently refractory.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Immunosuppressive Medications → Corticosteroids → rejection fever
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Cytokine release is responsible for the fever often associated with acute rejection

references.locator: Ch. 6 → Corticosteroids (cytokine-mediated fever in acute rejection); PDF p. 151 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Fourth 030200 item; anchor verified on Danovitch p. 151.

stem: After a solid-organ transplant, when must a transplant hospital collect organ-specific transplant recipient registration (TRR) data to meet OPTN timely data standards?

options.text: By recipient hospital discharge or 42 days after the transplant date, whichever is first
Only on the five-year transplant anniversary
Within 30 days of the match run date only
Never; TRR forms are optional for transplant hospitals

explanation.rationale_correct: OPTN Policy 18.2 requires timely TRR data collection by the transplant hospital when the recipient is discharged or by 42 days following the transplant date, whichever occurs first.

rationale_incorrect.B: Initial TRR collection is required early after transplant, not only at five years.
rationale_incorrect.C: Thirty days from match run applies to organ-offer outcome reporting responsibilities, not the TRR discharge window.
rationale_incorrect.D: TRR submission is a required timely data element for transplant hospitals.

primary_anchor.section: Policy 18.2 → Table 18-2 Timely Data Collection → TRR
primary_anchor.quote_hint: discharged from the hospital or 42 days following the transplant date, whichever is first

references.locator: Policy 18.2 → Table 18-2 Timely Data Collection (organ-specific transplant recipient registration [TRR]); PDF p. 334 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Third 030800 item; OPTN TRR timing distinct from cctc-3005/3019; anchor verified on optn-policies p. 334.

stem: During long-term follow-up teaching, a solid-organ recipient asks how common post-transplant diabetes mellitus is in the early months. What counseling is MOST accurate?

options.text: Diabetes may develop in up to about half of recipients within the first three months
Diabetes never occurs after transplantation because immunosuppression prevents it
Diabetes appears only after ten years and never in the first year
Post-transplant diabetes requires no monitoring because it cannot affect long-term outcomes

explanation.rationale_correct: Diabetes after transplantation may occur in up to 50% of solid organ transplant recipients within the first three months and worsens long-term outcomes, requiring monitoring and management.

rationale_incorrect.B: Immunosuppression, including corticosteroids and CNIs, contributes to post-transplant diabetes rather than preventing it.
rationale_incorrect.C: Post-transplant diabetes is common in the early post-transplant period, not exclusively after a decade.
rationale_incorrect.D: Post-transplant diabetes decreases quality of life and worsens long-term outcomes, so monitoring is required.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 4, Immunosuppression → C. Medications to manage DM → 2.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: DM after transplantation occurs in up to 50% of solid organ transplant recipients within the first 3 months

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 4 → C. Medications to manage DM → 2. (DM after transplantation occurs in up to 50% of solid organ transplant recipients within the first 3 months); PDF p. 161 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).
